 The 30 percent federal credit is gone, and nobody pays you for surplus
 Two corrections that several competing comparisons still get wrong, and both make kits look cheaper than they are.
 The 30 percent residential clean energy credit ended on December 31, 2025. Any page that quietly knocks 30 percent off a 2026 price is quoting a rebate that no longer exists. A $499 kit costs $499.
 And there is no export credit. As of August 16, 2026 no enacted state law grants net metering, an export payment, or any compensation at all for surplus from a plug-in device. Every kilowatt-hour your kit makes while the house is empty leaves through the meter and earns nothing. That single fact, not the brand, is what decides whether a larger kit is worth the money, which is why the sizing question belongs in the savings calculator rather than in a product table.
 Which configuration suits which household
 There is no single best plug-in solar kit, because the constraint that decides it is your building and your schedule, not the hardware.
 Renting, with a railing and a no-drilling lease. The 180 watt single-panel kit is the shape that fits. It is light (the panels are listed at 11 pounds each and 46 by 34 inches), it is designed to go up with zip ties, it uses an inverter with room for a second panel later, and it is the cheapest way to find out whether your balcony gets the sun you think it does. Get landlord permission in writing first, and read the renter’s guide on what a lease can and cannot restrict.
 Owning, with a patio, a fence or a south-facing wall. You can tilt, which is worth roughly a third more output than the same panel hung vertically, and you are not asking anyone’s permission. Here the oversized DC approach pays: buy to your state’s AC cap, then put more panel watts behind it than the cap suggests. Panels are the cheap part of that equation and inverter capacity is the regulated part.
 Home during the day. Someone working from home, retired, or running a fridge and a home office through the afternoon converts nearly everything a kit makes into avoided purchases. Buy the largest AC output your state allows and skip the battery. This is the household where the economics are genuinely straightforward.
 Out of the house from eight to six. This is the hard case, and it is where a battery unit like the STREAM Ultra earns its price or fails to. The battery makes no extra energy, it moves midday production into the evening so you actually consume it. Whether that is worth roughly a thousand dollars over a panels-only kit depends on your rate, your evening load and how steep your time-of-use spread is. A smaller kit sized to your daytime baseline (the always-on floor of fridge, router and standby draw) is often the better first purchase.
 Buying questions
 What is the best plug-in solar kit for a home in 2026?
 There is no single answer, because availability is the binding constraint. As of August 16, 2026 we could verify only two grid-connected families on sale to US buyers from the maker’s own store: EcoFlow’s STREAM products and Bright Saver’s Hoymiles-based kits. Choose between them on rated AC output against your state’s cap, on whether the seller ships to your state, and on what the price includes, in that order.
 Are Anker, Jackery and Bluetti balcony solar systems sold in the United States?
 Not as grid-connected plug-in systems, as far as we could verify on August 16, 2026. Anker SOLIX’s US catalog lists portable panels from $79.99 for 30 W to $699.99 for 400 W with no grid-tied micro-inverter. Jackery’s HomePower balcony set is sold in Europe. Bluetti launched its Balco line in May 2026 at European prices, built to the European 800 watt feed-in limit. Portable power stations from any of these makers are legal everywhere, because they never connect to house wiring.
 How many watts should a balcony solar kit be?
 Start from your state’s AC cap, then from how much power your home actually draws while the sun is up. Utah and Maryland cap qualifying devices at 1,200 watts AC, Colorado allows 1,920 watts per address, and most states have no plug-in pathway at all. Because no state pays for surplus, a kit sized above your midday baseline load gives away the difference.
 Does a plug-in solar kit come with mounting hardware?
 Usually not, and this is the most common surprise in the total cost. Bright Saver’s kits ship with instructions for zip ties or screws rather than a bracket. EcoFlow’s US listings for the STREAM units do not include panels or a mount at the prices quoted here, and we could not find a US railing bracket listed on its store when we checked on August 16, 2026, though it sells purpose-built balcony brackets in Europe.
 Do plug-in solar panels still qualify for the 30 percent federal tax credit?
 No. The federal residential clean energy credit expired on December 31, 2025. Comparisons that still show a post-credit price for a 2026 kit are quoting a rebate that no longer exists, and the effect is to understate the real cost by nearly a third.
 Is UL 1741 or UL 3700 the certification to look for on a kit?
 UL 3700 is the standard written for this product, covering the panel, plug and system together, while UL 1741 covers the inverter as a piece of equipment. As of August 16, 2026 no enacted state law names UL 3700 by number, so a UL 1741 listed device satisfies every current statute. Watch the wording on the box: “compliant” is a manufacturer’s claim, while “listed” points to a laboratory finding you can look up.
 Do this in order, and it takes an evening. Confirm what your state allows and what the AC cap is. Open the manufacturer’s spec sheet, not a retail listing, and write down the rated AC output and the exact certification sentence. Check the seller’s shipping restrictions against your address. Price the mount separately and confirm it fits your railing. Then put your own electricity rate and your own daytime occupancy into the calculator and see whether the answer still appeals. If a seller will not tell you which standard the unit was tested to, or will not quote a mount, you have learned something useful for free.
